verdict: Same face, same 30px cap height, same #1C1C1C ink, same 3px blue caret filling exactly one line box — this comes down to where the line starts, and A gets it wrong. Every heading and every list item in A jogs two or three characters to the right of the paragraph edge, so the column's left margin stutters down the page as you write; you notice it on the first heading and never stop noticing it. B parks the hashes and dashes in the margin and keeps one true edge, at the cost of markers I'd lift two steps lighter. A's extra pitch (38 vs 37 CSS px at the identical cap height) is the one thing it holds over B — and since both are on the same size step, one of those two pitches is off its rung.

states.name: quattro
states.gap: Syntax furniture is set at #7A7A7A (4.2:1 on #F9F9F9) against B's #9E9E9E (2.4:1) — the inline `*…*` and `**bottle**` sit only ~94 grey levels off the #1C1C1C prose and are the same grey as the list dash, so emphasis markup speckles the middle of a sentence instead of receding; A's heading text also overhangs its own rail by 6px (3 CSS px, 617 vs body 623).
states.gapTheirs: Markers are in the text flow, not hung: every `#`/`##` and `- ` sits at x=622 with the body, pushing heading and list text to x=667/668 — a 45–46px (≈23 CSS px, one full character cell) step right of the body edge, so the left rail reads as three different edges down the page; A hangs its markers right-aligned into the gutter (cells ending at 595) and keeps heading, body and list text flush at ~620.
states.verdict: A holds one flush left edge for every line of actual prose and puts the markdown scaffolding in the margin where it belongs; B lets a hash and a dash shove the words you wrote 23px to the right, so headings and list items never line up with the paragraph under them. B buys back a little quiet with fainter #9E9E9E markers, then breaks its own rule by leaving the list dash at #7A7A7A — two greys for the same class of punctuation, visible in the same screenful. A's grid is also exact where B's drifts: A's paragraph and heading gaps are 148px, precisely 2×74 pitch, while B's are 151–152 against a 76px pitch, about a pixel of slop per block. A's own sin is that its asterisks and hashes are three shades too insistent, but a dark marker in the margin costs less than a ragged column.

states.name: mono
states.gap: Harshest ink/page pair of the two: body at #1c1c1c on a flat #f9f9f9 page = 16.0:1 contrast, ~45% more than B's #cdcdcd on #1a1a1a (11.1:1), and the type is set 1.6% larger (advance 26.01px vs 25.60px, cap 30px vs 29px) for no gain — it just costs ~3 characters of measure, wrapping at ~62 chars where B holds ~65 in the same column.
states.gapTheirs: Syntax markers are the same ink as the prose: the heading '#' is bold, 5px stems at #cccccc — byte-identical in value to 'The Lighthouse' beside it — and the italic '*' delimiters render at the same #cdcdcd as the italic run, so '*Nothing' and 'hurry,*' read as punctuation in the sentence. A dims both to #7a7a7a at 2px regular-weight stems (4.1:1 against its page vs 16:1 for prose), so they recede.
states.verdict: Same typeface, same true italic, same 4px body stems — so the whole decision rests on two things, and B loses both. B's baselines land at 208.5, 282.5, 355.5, 428.5, 501.5: a 74px gap followed by three 73px gaps, i.e. a fractional ~73.25px pitch that cannot sit on the pixel grid, where A repeats 74.00px exactly five times with zero drift; you feel that as a column that will not hold still under a scroll. Worse, B leaves the '#' bold and full-strength, so every heading you type reads as '# The Lighthouse' rather than a title, and the asterisks around the father's line sit in the sentence at full ink like stray glyphs. A's page is the glarier surface and buys three fewer characters per line with its extra 1.6% of size, but that is a preference; B's markers and wobbling pitch are mistakes.

B's page carries +/-1 RGB per-channel grain around #1a1a1a (730 unique colours in a 400x40 empty patch vs A's single flat #f9f9f9) — chroma speckle under the type, invisible at 100% but there
Italics are genuine cut italics in both, not obliqued roman; ink coverage per line is near-identical (A 15.6%, B 16.6%), so neither blooms noticeably
